subject: science
title: KS3 / Year 7-9 Science - Atoms, Elements and Compounds
subtitle: Key KS3 chemistry ideas about particles, formulae, pure substances, mixtures and evidence for chemical change.
description: This source-faithful KS3 chemistry pack revises atoms, elements, compounds, mixtures, formulae, particle diagrams and the periodic table. It also practises evidence-based classification, physical separation, chemical change, and common misconceptions such as confusing molecules with compounds or mixtures with pure substances.

data.title: Reading H2O
data.instruction: Put the steps for interpreting H2O in the correct order.
items: Identify H as hydrogen and O as oxygen.
Notice that the small 2 belongs to H.
Recognise that no small number after O means one oxygen atom.
State that one water molecule contains two hydrogen atoms and one oxygen atom.
Conclude that water is a compound because different elements are chemically joined.

data.title: Iron and Sulfur Reaction
data.instruction: Order the events when iron and sulfur are heated strongly.
items: Grey iron filings and yellow sulfur powder are mixed together.
A magnet can attract the iron while it is still a mixture.
The mixture is heated strongly in a controlled practical.
The mixture glows and becomes very hot.
A black solid called iron sulfide forms.
The product cannot be separated with a magnet in the same simple way.

data.title: Separating Sand and Salt
data.instruction: Put the separation method for sand and salt in the correct order.
items: Add water so the salt dissolves but the sand does not.
Filter the mixture so the sand stays in the filter paper.
Collect the salt solution that passes through the filter.
Evaporate the water from the salt solution.
Recover the salt left behind after evaporation.

data.title: Using Evidence to Classify a Sample
data.instruction: Order the reasoning process for classifying an unknown sample.
items: Observe the appearance of the sample carefully.
Choose simple tests such as magnet testing, filtration or evaporation.
Record observations in a clear table.
Decide whether a new substance formed or whether substances separated physically.
Use the evidence to classify the sample as an element, compound or mixture.
